title: Graceful tenant throttling and reservation flexibility PRD
creator: Aisha Patel
description: Problem: Customers on Dedicated capacity sometimes overshoot their reserved throughput for short spiky windows. Current options (hard eviction, preemption to lower tiers, or outright rejection) produce abrupt degradation for tenant-facing SLAs and increase support noise. We need a controlled, configurable way to gracefully throttle tenants during transient oversubscription while preserving bounded latency and predictable billing behavior. This PRD defines a feature set called "tenant shaping and reservation flexibility" focused on: (1) configurable soft-throttles that shape request pacing when a tenant exceeds reserves, (2) temporary reservation flexibility to allow short, metered burst above commit, and (3) observability and console controls for SLO alignment and auditing.
goals: Provide a soft-throttle mechanism that reduces request forwarding rate for an over-quota tenant instead of hard rejection
Introduce controlled temporary burst capacity that can be metered and billed differently from committed capacity
Surface tenant shaping policies and runtime state in the Console and API for operators and customers
Allow operators to configure per-tenant shaping profiles (latency targets, burst window, degradation strategy) and enable safe defaults
Ensure rollout with canary and metrics-driven guardrails to avoid platform-wide regression
non_goals: Replacing existing hard preemption/eviction flows for sustained overloads
Designing new billing primitives beyond metered burst charges (billing integration is limited to metered counters in this phase)
Full multi-region cross-tenant migration or refugee scheduling — out of scope for initial launch
requirements: Functional: Ability to define per-tenant shaping policy with: baseline reserved RPS, soft-burst allowance (tokens or time-window), shaping algorithm (leaky-bucket or token-bucket), and degradation action (queue, delay, reduce tokens, or degrade to lower QoS)
Functional: API & Console: Expose a Policy object in the admin API and a Console page to view/edit tenant shaping profiles and live state
Functional: Metering: Emit metered metrics for 'burst consumed', 'shaping applied', and 'requests delayed' with 1s resolution to billing and observability pipelines
Functional: Runtime: Implement low-latency enforcement inside the request router before scheduling work on GPUs to avoid wasted KV cache and kernel preparation
Non-functional: P99 latency for reserved baseline requests should not regress more than 10% in steady-state under shaping enabled
Non-functional: Shaping decisions must add no more than 2ms median overhead to request admission path
Security/Compliance: All changes must preserve tenant isolation; no cross-tenant data leakage allowed
Operational: Provide operator toggles: global ON/OFF, per-tenant override, and emergency bypass for SRE
acceptance_criteria: Can define and persist a shaping policy via API and Console for a tenant (create/read/update/delete)
When tenant exceeds reserved RPS by a short burst, router applies configured soft-throttle instead of immediate 429s; observed in live traffic during synthetic tests
Billing pipeline receives burst-consumption counters for metered charge reconciliation (test export shows counters for synthetic tenant)
Observability: Console shows live shaping state and historical chart (burst consumed per minute, requests delayed per minute) for the tenant

Performance: Under a controlled 2x burst test (2x reserved RPS sustained for 30s), 95% of reserved-priority requests remain within 1.5x baseline latency and platform resource efficiency improves vs immediate preemption
Safety: Canary rollout to 5% of tenants does not increase platform error budget or cause cross-tenant interference over 48 hours
Operator controls work: global OFF and per-tenant hard override immediately stops shaping within 5s
success_metrics: Reduced 429 rate for short bursts by >= 60% for tenants enabled with shaping
Billing accuracy: burst-metering counters within 0.5% of request logs in reconciliation tests
Operator MTTR: reduce capacity-related incidents with noisy tenants by 30% within first quarter
Adoption: 25% of newly provisioned Dedicated tenants opt into default shaping profile within 3 months
Latency: p99 for baseline traffic when shaping active <= baseline_p99 * 1.10 across canary sample
rollout_plan: Design review and API spec (2 weeks) — define minimal Policy schema and Console UX
Runtime prototype behind feature flag (3 weeks) — token-bucket shaping implemented in router with telemetry
Internal dogfood on non-production cluster (1 week) — iterate on metrics and overhead
Canary to 5% production tenants for 48–72 hours with tight monitoring and rollback playbook
Expand to 25% over two weeks if metrics stable, then full launch with documentation and billing update
Post-launch: 30-day observational period and retrospective to tune defaults
dependencies: Metrics pipeline work to accept new burst metering counters (ENG-59112)
Billing team support for reading burst counters and adding metered item (Finance-ops ticket)
Console UI: new tenant policy editor component (DES-12009)
risks: Incorrect shaping parameters could silently increase latency for high-priority requests — mitigate by conservative defaults and telemetry
Metering mismatch between router counters and billing could cause disputes — mitigate by reconciliation tests and idempotent counters
Operator misuse (overly permissive burst) could reduce isolation — mitigate with guardrail limits and approval flows for high burst ceilings
Performance overhead in admission path may affect overall p99 if not optimized — mitigate via microbenchmarks and limit of <2ms added overhead
open_questions: Should burst be billed per-token (generation tokens) or per-RPS window for the initial launch? (tradeoffs: accuracy vs billing complexity)
What is the canonical default shaping policy for new tenants on Dedicated? (suggested: 10% sustained, 3x for 30s burst window)
How should shaping interact with model-variant fallback (e.g., if cheaper variant available, should requests be routed instead of throttled)?
What audit trail is required for compliance customers to prove no silent denial-of-service happened?
